complexity_matrix.operation: Comparison of two keys in the decision tree
complexity_matrix.notes: One branch per level. Total comparisons are what the n!-leaves argument bounds.
Linear in the combined run length; each element is emitted exactly once.
Theta(n log n) on every input, which is the reason it is the safe default. Aux space is one reused scratch buffer.
One linear pass in place. This is the unit of work, not the algorithm.
Expected depth is O(log n); randomisation removes dependence on input order, so the worst case matches expectation in expectation.

complexity_matrix.operation: Quicksort with a deterministic first-element pivot on sorted input
complexity_matrix.notes: Recurrence becomes T(n) = T(n-1) + Theta(n). Also recurses n deep, so it can exhaust the native stack.
Quadratic, and kept only for small ranges or adaptive use.

complexity_matrix.operation: Insertion sort on already sorted input
complexity_matrix.notes: Adaptive: each pass finds the insertion point immediately. This is why hybrids use it below n ~ 16.
k is the key range. Performs no comparisons at all, which is how it escapes the n log n barrier.

complexity_matrix.operation: Radix sort, d passes over fixed-width keys
complexity_matrix.notes: d is the digit count. Each pass is a stable counting sort on one digit.
The only in-place sort with a worst-case n log n guarantee, at the cost of the worst memory access pattern.

complexity_matrix.operation: Comparison lower bound for any comparison sort
complexity_matrix.notes: n! orderings need n! leaves; a depth-k binary tree has at most 2^k. Attained, so this is optimal rather than merely best-known.

correctness_argument.claim: Mergesort is correct by induction on run length: two sorted runs merge into a sorted sequence because the smaller front element is always the minimum of the union. Quicksort is correct because partitioning places every element at or before the pivot in order, so sorting each side sorts the whole. Counting sort is correct only because the prefix sum gives the exact count of keys below each key, an assumption that is invalid outside a bounded range.

cost_derivations.claim: Solving n! <= 2^k gives k >= ceil(log2(n!)) = Omega(n log n), and mergesort spends exactly that by paying Theta(n) at each of log2 n levels. Counting sort achieves Theta(n + k) by performing no comparisons, which is only sound when the key range is bounded.
cost_derivations.detail: Insertion sort is quadratic on random input but linear on sorted input, so its value is adaptivity rather than its bound.

limits.claim: No comparison sort can beat Omega(n log n) because the bound is a property of the problem class, not of an algorithm. Beating it requires leaving the comparison model entirely, as counting and radix sorts do, and paying for the key range in both time and space. Heapsort attains the optimal worst case with the worst memory access pattern of any comparison sort, which is why introsort runs quicksort and falls back to heapsort only at a depth limit.
